dedupe_keys.name: hawaii false ballistic missile alert and the fcc investigation 2018

description: This emergency-response and post-event case covers the false ballistic missile alert sent to the public in Hawaii on 13 January 2018 and the investigation of it by the Federal Communications Commission. At 8:07 a.m. local time a warning officer of the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency, taking part in an unannounced drill, sent a live alert through the Emergency Alert System, which reaches radio and television stations, and through Wireless Emergency Alerts to mobile phones. Transmission was stopped at 8:12, but the official correction through the same channels came only at 8:45, 38 minutes later, and 911 lines were overwhelmed with 7,755 calls against a normal 250 to 350. The FCC's Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau issued a preliminary report in January and a final report in April 2018, finding no technical fault in the alert systems but a mix of human error and weak safeguards: no second-person check, poor supervision of drills at shift change, software that did not clearly separate test and live alerts, and no plan for correcting a false alert. It made 24 recommendations on drill oversight, verification, pre-written corrections, software design and training. Coverage: one state, one event, with national lessons. Format and access: FCC reports as PDF and text, free. Caveats: the report relies on interviews and agency records; public reaction is studied separately, for example by the CDC. Simulation uses: emergency communication chains, human-error scenarios in alerting systems and operational procedures for public warning. Related records: the US nationwide alert test of 2023 examines the same alert chain.
